verdicts.why: Accepting someone's claim or authority is a plain act with no attitude toward them built into the verb.
Reporting receipt is a neutral clerical act; the word takes no side.
Accepting something as legally valid is a formal, descriptive act carrying no approval or contempt.
A statistical mean is a technical term with no attitude in it.
The postpositive 'the city proper' sense merely draws a boundary and judges nothing; the decorum sense in the sentences is a different synset.
Letting someone into a group is described without any stance toward them.
Granting the right to participate is a plain institutional act with no colouring.
A path or door that admits people is described physically, not judged.
Giving entrance to someone is neutral; nothing in the verb says how the speaker feels about them.
This is the plain institutional term for information-gathering, and it is 'spying' rather than 'intelligence' that carries the sneer.
The name of an organisational unit is descriptive, with no attitude toward it.
A gradual decline in amount is a plain quantity word; an unwelcome referent is not a loaded word.
Bereavement is a painful referent, but 'loss' is the plain word for it and does not add an attitude.
The accounting shortfall is a neutral technical term.
The gloss itself marks it euphemistic: choosing 'loss' over 'death' softens the blow and signals tact and sympathy toward the bereaved, which a learner needs to be told.
Military 'losses' is the standard tally word for personnel lost; grim referent, plain word.
A shade of colour is described, not judged.
Timbre is a neutral acoustic property; any attitude in the sentences comes from the adjectives attached to it.
A written note in musical notation carries no attitude.
Muscle tone is a physiological term with no evaluative charge in the word itself.
A whole-step interval is a technical music term, neutral by nature.
A pure steady sound is described in physical terms with no judgement.
The linguistic pitch feature is a technical term with no attitude.
Facts gathered by watching are named plainly; the word says nothing about the watcher's or speaker's stance.
Making and recording a measurement is a neutral scientific act.
